title: Linked list explained: singly and doubly linked lists, Python code and complexity — cv.cm
description: Learn how a linked list works: nodes and pointers, insert, delete, reverse and cycle detection in Python, with time complexity compared to arrays.
h1: Linked list explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node stores a value and a reference (pointer) to the next node. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored next to each other in memory, so inserting or removing a node at a known position takes O(1) time, but finding the k-th element takes O(n) because you must walk from the head. A doubly linked list also stores a pointer to the previous node.

sections.h: What problem a linked list solves
body: An array (a Python `list`) keeps its elements in one contiguous block of memory. Reading `a[i]` is instant, but inserting at the front shifts every other element one slot to the right, which costs O(n). A linked list avoids that shift: each element lives in its own node, and nodes are connected by references. To insert, you only change a couple of references.
Linked lists are the building block behind many other structures: stacks, queues, hash table buckets (separate chaining), LRU caches and adjacency lists in graphs.

Think of a treasure hunt: each clue tells you where the next clue is. You cannot jump to clue number 7; you must follow clues 1 to 6 first. The list itself only remembers the first node, called the head. The last node points to nothing (`None`).

body: Start with the list `3 -> 7 -> 9`. We insert 5 after 3, then delete 7.

ol: Create a new node with value 5.
Set `new.next` to the node after 3 (the node 7).
Set `node3.next` to the new node. The list is now `3 -> 5 -> 7 -> 9`.
To delete 7, find the node before it (5) by walking from the head.
Set `node5.next = node5.next.next`, which skips 7. The list is now `3 -> 5 -> 9`. Python's garbage collector frees the unreachable node.

body.note: The order of steps 2 and 3 matters. If you first set `node3.next = new`, you lose the only reference to the rest of the list.

sections.h: Python implementation of a singly linked list
body: This class keeps a reference to the head and a size counter. It supports adding at the front and back, deleting the first matching value, and iteration.

body.code:
items = LinkedList()
for x in [3, 7, 9]:
    items.push_back(x)
items.push_front(1)
items.remove(7)
print(list(items), items.size)  # [1, 3, 9] 3

body: `push_back` here walks the whole list, so it is O(n). Keeping an extra `tail` reference makes it O(1); that is what real queue implementations do.

sections.h: Classic operations: reverse and cycle detection
body: Reversing a list in place is the most common linked list interview question. Walk the list once and turn each `next` pointer around.

body.code:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next     # remember the rest
        cur.next = prev    # turn the pointer around
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev            # new head
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
head = reverse(head)
print(head.value, head.next.value, head.next.next.value)  # 3 2 1
print(has_cycle(head))  # False

body: `has_cycle` is Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm: a slow pointer moves one step and a fast pointer moves two steps. If there is a loop, the fast pointer eventually meets the slow one; if not, it reaches `None`. It uses O(1) extra memory.

body: In practice, arrays are often faster even for operations where the linked list has a better Big O, because array elements sit next to each other in memory and use the CPU cache well. Linked list nodes are scattered.

ul: Forgetting the empty list: always check `head is None` before reading `head.next`.
Losing the rest of the list by overwriting `next` before saving it (see `nxt` in `reverse`).
Not updating `head` when the first node is removed, or `tail` when the last node is removed.
Using recursion on very long lists: Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames, so iterative code is safer.
A dummy (sentinel) head node removes most special cases: every real node then has a previous node.
In a doubly linked list, every insert and delete must update four references; missing one corrupts the list silently.

sections.h: When to use a linked list, and what to use in Python
body: Use a linked list when you insert and remove at the ends or in the middle at positions you already hold a reference to, and you rarely need random access. Examples: an LRU cache (doubly linked list plus hash map), the free list of a memory allocator, undo history, or the buckets of a hash table.

In everyday Python code you rarely write your own. For a queue or deque, use `collections.deque`, which gives O(1) appends and pops at both ends. For general sequences, use `list`. Write your own linked list for learning, for interviews, and when you need to splice nodes in O(1), as in an LRU cache.

body.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2, 3])
q.appendleft(0)
q.append(4)
print(q.popleft(), q.pop(), list(q))  # 0 4 [1, 2, 3]

faq.q: Is a Python list a linked list?
faq.a: No. A Python `list` is a dynamic array of references stored contiguously, so indexing is O(1) and inserting at the front is O(n). `collections.deque` is the closest built-in to a linked list for queue use.

faq.q: Why is access in a linked list O(n)?
faq.a: Nodes are not stored at predictable addresses. The only way to reach the k-th node is to start at the head and follow k `next` references.

faq.q: When is a doubly linked list better than a singly linked list?
faq.a: When you need to delete a node given only a reference to it, or move backwards. With a `prev` pointer, deletion is O(1) without searching for the previous node, at the cost of one extra reference per node.

faq.q: How do you find the middle of a linked list in one pass?
faq.a: Use two pointers: move one by one step and the other by two steps. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle.

A dummy node placed before the first real node (and sometimes after the last). It holds no data, but it means every real node has a neighbor, so insert and delete code needs fewer special cases for the empty list and the head.
